parole.significato: Baptist (member of a Baptist church or denomination)
parole.testo: Borrowed from English Baptist, from Ancient Greek βαπτιστής (baptistḗs). By surface analysis, Ancient Greek βάπτω (báptō) + -и́ст (-íst).

parole.significato: electron (first-generation leptonic particle of negative charge)
parole.testo: Scientific term from English electron coined in 19th century. Morphologically formed as електри́чен (elektríčen, “electric”) + -он (-on). The suffix reflects the ending of Ancient Greek ἰόν (ión, “going, coming”) (whence Bulgarian йон (jon, “ion”)).

parole.testo: Borrowed from English Xerox (“a photocopier”), a genericized trademark, from Ancient Greek ξηρός (xērós, “dry”) and γραφή (graphḗ, “writing”).

Scientific term from English neutron coined in 20th century. Morphologically formed from the stem of неутра́лен (neutrálen, “neutral”) + -он (-on). The suffix reflects the ending of Ancient Greek ἰόν (ión, “going, coming”) (whence Bulgarian йон (jon, “ion”)).

parole.significato: positron (first-generation leptonic particle of positive charge; anti-doublet of electrons)
parole.testo: Scientific term from English positron coined in 20th century. Morphologically formed as позити́вен (pozitíven, “positive”) + -он (-on). The suffix reflects the ending of Ancient Greek ἰόν (ión, “going, coming”) (whence Bulgarian йон (jon, “ion”)).

Internationalism, originally coined as English chloride, from Ancient Greek χλωρός (khlōrós, “salt”). Possibly borrowed through German Chlorid, or perhaps Russian хлори́д (xloríd).
